note: Research behind the masthead drawings (20 Oct 2026). Each place was checked as open (or, for KFC Signal, what changed), local and iconic from dated sources; the brief is what the Figma drawing was generated from.

12th-main.name: 12th Main Road
12th-main.caption: 12th Main, HAL 2nd Stage
12th-main.why: This is Indiranagar's eating-out street. A residential layout road has become a nearly continuous strip of cafes, restaurants and pubs. A food blogger who has reviewed a run of its restaurants advises against walking in without a booking on weekend nights, and praises one place for keeping out the street's honking. It meets 100 Feet Road at one of the neighbourhood's busiest signal junctions.
12th-main.brief: Best view: looking west along 12th Main toward the 100 Feet Road signal. Near the junction, very large old shade trees with wide umbrella crowns and long level limbs arch over the road from both sides and almost close over it. They look like rain trees; check on site. A low concrete median splits the road, with cars parked nose to tail along it. On the eastern stretch, a line of green-and-yellow autorickshaws is parked along the median. Foreground: a scooter rider, a stray dog trotting across, and a few people standing on the corner pavement beside a small kiosk hung with strips of snack packets. At the junction there is a traffic signal on a pole and shopfronts with signboards. A March 2026 community photo also shows a small sloping tiled roof right beside the signal. Looking east, the two sides differ: on the south side a glass-fronted 4-storey block; on the north side a shopfront, then an older house behind a compound wall and iron gate, with a coconut palm. Utility poles carry bundles of cable. In February-March, pink trumpet trees (Tabebuia, probably T. rosea) at the junction and along the road flower pale pink while nearly leafless (community photos from late Feb and late Mar 2026). Optional period figure: a photo from 13 Jan 2009, titled 'Indiranagar 12th Main', shows a seller in a red cap and red T-shirt holding up magazines and a food guide to cars and motorbikes stopped at a signal under a big tree canopy. Shop boards stay blank.

indiranagar-metro-station.name: Indiranagar metro station (Purple Line)
indiranagar-metro-station.caption: Indiranagar metro station, CMH Road
indiranagar-metro-station.why: It opened on 20 October 2011 as one of Namma Metro's first six stations, and the first section of the city's metro to run was the one through Indiranagar. For most visitors it is the way into the neighbourhood. It sits just off the junction of the two main roads, 100 Feet Road and CMH Road.
indiranagar-metro-station.brief: An elevated station that straddles CMH Road about 150-200 m west of the 100 Feet Road junction. The station sits on pairs of ochre-yellow columns joined by cross-beams, so traffic and autos pass straight underneath on either side of a planted median. The viaduct curves in from 100 Feet Road with a pipe railing along its edge. Above, a long shed roof on curved steel trusses and blue-grey steel columns covers two side platforms. The trains are silver with a thin purple stripe; the platform makes a good inset or second drawing. At street level, a line of green-and-yellow autorickshaws waits under the viaduct, and close rows of scooters and motorbikes are parked in front of the shops. A large shade tree stands on the pavement, with 3-4 storey shop buildings behind carrying stacked signboards (draw them blank).

glens-bakehouse.name: Glen's Bakehouse
glens-bakehouse.caption: Glen's Bakehouse, 100 Feet Road
glens-bakehouse.why: This is the owner's own reference: a white converted house with a tiled porch and a wrought-iron arched gate on 100 Feet Road, next door to Toit. With 14,463 Google reviews it is one of the city's best-known bakeries, and EazyDiner (4 Aug 2026) calls it 'One of the most popular bakehouse chains in Bangalore'.
glens-bakehouse.brief: Viewpoint: straight on from the 100 Feet Road pavement, looking west. The concrete metro pillar (P63) can frame the left edge. A white two-storey converted house. Upper storey: a plain white block under a thin, flat, overhanging roof slab on visible rafters. At upper left, the GLEN'S BAKEHOUSE name sits in an ornate oval badge (draw the name only). At right, a small window with open wooden shutters under a little hood. A low terracotta-tiled lean-to porch roof runs across the ground floor. In the centre it is broken by a white rendered round arch holding an open, ornate white wrought-iron scroll gate. Through the arch you see an exposed-brick wall and warm hanging lamps. There is a wall lantern on each side of the arch. Low white walls topped with scrolling wrought-iron railings run along both sides. At left: potted conifers and a market umbrella. Right of the arch: a lit standing signboard (name only). In front: a stone-slab path, with scooters parked at right. Behind at left rises a tall Norfolk pine. Draw it at dusk with the porch lamps glowing, as in the owner's photo. Optional: Street View (Dec 2025) shows two later details, black line-art bakery murals on the upper walls with a red star on the corner, and a word ('JIREH') lettered on the arch crown. Both can be left out at small size.
sources: Owner's photo of the frontage (sent in chat, 20 Oct 2026)

toit.name: Toit Brewpub
toit.caption: Toit, 100 Feet Road
toit.why: Toit opened on 100 Feet Road in 2010 and is Bengaluru's best-known brewpub. Onmanorama says it 'gained iconic status among beer enthusiasts', and it has 62,775 Google reviews. Its steep wooden A-frame roof under the metro is instantly recognisable.
toit.brief: Viewpoint: a three-quarter view from the south-east, on the 100 Feet Road kerb. A fat fluted metro pillar and the underside of the elevated viaduct cross the top left. Left: Toit's signature steep A-frame roof, sloping almost to the ground. Its sloped faces are covered in a wooden trellis lattice, and a big round TOIT disc sign sits in the gable (name only). Below it, an open shopfront with green-framed glass doors and a counter. Right: a three-storey dark steel-and-glass block. It has a red exposed-brick panel on the first floor, AC units, a lattice-screened rooftop and a tall vertical green-wall panel on its edge. At street level: a bamboo-slat screen fence with a round sign, brick planters, dense palms that hide part of the front, bicycles, bollards and a waiting crowd. Draw it in the evening with warm lights.

chokkanathaswamy-temple.name: Shri Chokkanathaswamy Temple, Domlur
chokkanathaswamy-temple.caption: Chokkanathaswamy Temple, Domlur
chokkanathaswamy-temple.why: Inscriptions in Epigraphia Carnatica make this Domlur temple at least as old as 1200 CE, and Wikipedia's list of Chola temples, citing Deccan Herald, calls it the oldest temple in the city. It sits on Indiranagar's south-west edge, and Google even gives its address as 2nd Stage Indiranagar.
chokkanathaswamy-temple.brief: Based on Google Street View (Mar 2026) from the end of narrow Rama Temple Road, looking west at the east-facing front. The temple stands on a high stone plinth, reached by granite steps with steel handrails. On top is a flat-roofed entrance hall with square stone pillars and a deep cornice. Along its roofline runs a parapet of small painted stucco deity figures, rising in the centre to a small tiered tower with kalasha finials. A wide name board spans the entrance (blank or name only). The metal grille gates are decorated with the U-shaped Vaishnava namam mark. To the right, a compound wall painted in vertical red-and-white temple stripes (alternating stripes in ink). To the left, small shopfronts and houses. Behind: a tall coconut palm, a large leafy tree and newer apartment blocks. Scooters are parked at the foot of the steps, with a devotee or two. Soft early-morning light. Caution: a 2021 Wikimedia Commons front view shows the steps as twin flights meeting at a central landing, with a tall square stone lamp pillar on the platform. Check the 2026 Street View link before drawing the stair.

bobs-bar.name: Bob's Bar (Indiranagar flagship)
bobs-bar.caption: Bob's Bar, 100 Feet Road
bobs-bar.why: Time Out (7 Jan 2026) says 'Bob's is an institution' and that the 100 Feet Road original 'still has the most charm'. It is an old house under a huge rain tree, and it has about 21,000 Google reviews.
bobs-bar.brief: Based on Street View (Mar 2026), from the 100 Feet Road footpath looking west. At street level a long, low white compound wall curves gently inward between square white gateposts, each topped with a round globe lamp. The bar's name is painted on the wall in Kannada script (blank or name only), beside a small black stone house-name plaque (blank). Behind the wall is an older two-storey house, mostly hidden under a huge spreading rain tree whose trunk and canopy fill the upper right. On the first floor, a timber pergola frame holds a sagging canvas roof over terrace seating, with lanterns glowing underneath. To the left stands a taller neighbouring building with arched upper windows and a metal-grille gate. In front: concrete paving, a planter bed of shrubs and a young tree, a bicycle leaning on the wall, and scooters at the kerb. Draw it in the evening with the terrace lanterns lit.

kfc-signal.name: KFC Signal
kfc-signal.caption: KFC Signal, 100 Feet Road & CMH Road (KFC till 2025)
kfc-signal.why: KFC Signal is what locals call the traffic signal where 100 Feet Road crosses CMH (Chinmaya Mission Hospital) Road. The name comes from the KFC, with a Pizza Hut upstairs, in the building on the south-west corner, whose giant bucket sign stood over the junction. Wikipedia names the bus stop on both roads 'Indiranagar Police station/KFC signal' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiranagar,_Bengaluru). An October 2012 meetup gave directions to the 100ft Road–CMH Road junction, marked (KFC) (https://trailblazercommunitygroups.com/events/details/salesforce-bengaluru-salesforce-developer-group-presents-bangalore-forcecom-october-meetup/). exchange4media (18 Nov 2025) calls the bucket a wayfinder and a city-wide reference point (https://www.exchange4media.com/out-of-home-news/blurus-iconic-kfc-signal-makes-way-for-pizza-hut-the-media-value-of-brand-landmarks-149431.html).
kfc-signal.status:
changed: KFC left the corner in November 2025 and its bucket sign was removed. The building now holds a SNITCH clothing store with the Pizza Hut still upstairs. The junction keeps its old name on Google Maps, and SNITCH promotes 'SNITCH Signal'.

(1) X post by @tarinisarah, 15 Nov 2025: a photo shows only the Pizza Hut, captioned that the signal lost its KFC (https://twitter.com/tarinisarah/status/1989673674140782927). Reported by Curly Tales, 17 Nov 2025 (https://curlytales.com/bengaluru/trending/bengaluru-bids-goodbye-to-kfc-signal-in-indirangar-netizens-imagine-saying-pizza-hut-signal/).
(2) NewsKar
kfc-signal.brief:
Era: the last KFC look, before KFC left in mid-November 2025. Drawn from Annnu's Google Maps photo (Sep 2025, verified in the photo viewer). The junction layout comes from Street View pano TA0bd4 (Dec 2025), which was taken after KFC left. Use that pano only for the layout, the signal and the viaduct, not for the building's signage.

Viewpoint: the south-east corner by CornerStone Park, looking west-north-west across 100 Feet Road.

Left of frame: the end of an orange-and-glass neighbour building. Then the boxy corner block: about three storeys, with a flat roof and a thin metal frame along the roof edge.
- Top band: a dark fascia with the Pizza Hut name in plain lettering, with a red band beneath it.
- Below that, a strip of blue glass framed in red.
- The lower two floors are clad in vertical wood-look slats, with KFC in white letters on the left.
- A tall red portal frame runs from a first-floor window, past a grey slatted panel, down to the ground-floor shopfront.
- A coconut palm rises in front of the left wall.
- At its foot, a mesh-fenced electrical transformer and some shrubs.

On the street corner, a big white bucket sits above the red-framed corner door. It is slightly tapered, with a rolled rim and one red vertical stripe; draw it plain, with no logo or Colonel. Steps with steel handrails climb to the corner door.

At the kerb stand a tall streetlight and a signal pole. The pole has a cantilever arm, a three-lamp head and a green direction board.

Centre and right: CMH Road runs away west, with the grey Purple Line viaduct crossing it in the middle distance. A big rain tree stands on the left (south) side of CMH Road, just past the building. On the right is the NW-corner shop block: two to three storeys with a grey box upper floor and phone-shop fronts at street level, drawn as plain storefronts. Autos, scooters and a hatchback fill the road under midday sun.
kfc-signal.cautions:
1. The place has changed. KFC left this corner in mid-November 2025, and the bucket sign came down. KFC now trades at 538 CMH Road, about 240 m west. The building today is a SNITCH store, with the Pizza Hut still upstairs and still open. A drawing with the bucket shows the past, so the caption should say so, as the suggested one does.

2. The name is contested. SNITCH is publicly pushing 'SNITCH Signal' (exchange4media, Dec 2025; Franchise TV, Apr 2026). Google Maps still labels the junction 'KFC Signal Indiranagar', and November 2025 coverage quotes people saying the old name will stick. I found no independent 2026 evidence of which name locals use now.

3. Trademarks are heavy here. The KFC bucket with its red stripe and the Colonel portrait, and the Pizza Hut roof logo, are brand marks. Draw names only: plain lettering for KFC and Pizza Hut, a plain bucket with one stripe, no Colonel face, and no logos.

4. Dates of the look:
- The wood-slat front with the bucket comes from a September 2025 photo.
- January 2022 Street View shows an older red KFC fascia. A tree blocks the corner in that view, so I could not tell whether the bucket was there then, and its install date is unknown.
- The September 2019 photo shows yet another signage scheme.
- All December 2025 Street View is from after KFC left: the building is wrapped in SNITCH hoardings, and bunting hangs over the road. I used those panoramas only for the junction layout, the signal and the viaduct.

5. Google Maps puts the pin for the closed KFC listing about 240 m west, beside the new outlet, not at the junction. Its address and photos match the corner building. Use 12.97836, 77.64083 for any map pin.

6. Seen from the north-east corner looking south-west, the viaduct is hidden behind the north-west buildings. That is why the brief uses the south-east viewpoint.

humming-tree.name: The Humming Tree
humming-tree.caption: The Humming Tree, 100 Feet Road
humming-tree.why: The Humming Tree is a live-music venue and bar that Nikhil Barua founded in Indiranagar in 2013. It hosted gigs, theatre, comedy and film screenings, with acts from Skrillex and The Vaccines to Prateek Kuhad (https://rollingstoneindia.com/humming-tree-bengaluru-closure/ ; https://homegrown.co.in/homegrown-explore/the-humming-tree-20-what-the-iconic-venues-revival-means-for-indias-indie-landscape). Its first home was the 3rd floor and rooftop of No. 949, 12th Main. That venue closed in September 2019 after licensing trouble. It reopened in 2026 in a new building at 763, 100 Feet Road, listed as 12,000 sq ft with room for 600+ people (https://bangalore.explocity.com/events-in-bangalore/hg-music-showcase-reble-rae-mulla-more/).
humming-tree.status:
changed: OLD 12th MAIN VENUE: CLOSED.
- Wild City (2 Jun 2014) and Rolling Stone India (6 Jun 2014) report the first-birthday festival on 6–8 June 2014, so it opened around mid-2013: https://www.thewildcity.com/news/1508-the-humming-tree-to-celebrate-its-first-birthday ; https://rollingstoneindia.com/humming-tree-celebrates-one-year-anniversary/
- Rolling Stone India (19 Sep 2019) says it was to shut at the end of September 2019 because of building, licence and resident-complaint problems: https://rollingstoneindia.com/humming-tree-bengaluru-closure/
- Several later listings say the original run was 20
humming-tree.brief:
Source: Google Street View pano xh5moJC0BH8zLNK24te1vg at 763, 100 Feet Road, image capture March 2026, looking west-northwest. The gable and emblem details are checked against a Google Maps visitor photo from February 2026.

Draw it from the 100 Feet Road footpath at eye level.

Across the front runs a tall boundary wall, about one and a half times a person's height. It is clad in thin slate-to-charcoal brick tiles laid in fine horizontal courses. Along the wall runs the venue's name in raised white Kannada letters (ದಿ ಹಮ್ಮಿಂಗ್ ಟ್ರೀ). Do not swap in English.

To the right of the name is an upright, arch-topped, backlit plaque:
- a pale tree with a full, rounded canopy;
- a row of tiny silhouetted performers under the canopy;
- a small rectangular nameplate reading THE HUMMING TREE in serif capitals;
- roots fanning out below.
This is the brand logo, so keep it simple and generic.

Under the lettering, on the footpath in front of the wall, a grey metal electrical cabinet stands on a low concrete plinth. It is about head height, with a flat overhanging lid and graffiti on its door. Right of the emblem stand an electricity pole with a junction box and a tangle of cables, then a dark grey gate pillar with two pale notice boards. A plain pale plastered wall closes the left end of the frontage.

A large dark rectangular panel sits directly on top of the wall, at about first-floor level. A single row of round marquee bulbs frames it.

Behind the panel rises the main hall. It is a steep, house-shaped A-frame gable outlined by a thick warm-brown, timber-look border, with a dark face and a tall steel-gridded window. To its left is an open steel-frame grid; to its right, a flat steel pergola.

In the foreground, a big old roadside tree throws a thick, low limb diagonally across the scene, in front of the gable. Black cylindrical bollards with slanted tops line the kerb, and a few people walk by. On the left is the tall glass-fronted retail block next door, with wide steps.

It is daytime, with dappled shade.

Note: Subko opened a café here around September 2026 and may have added signage that this March 2026 imagery does not show.
humming-tree.cautions:
1. Which venue to draw. The 12th Main venue has been closed since September 2019. The bar now on its old floors at No. 949 is The Reservoire, and the building has been re-clad. The Humming Tree is open again at 763, 100 Feet Road. That is why the caption and drawing brief cover the current venue. I could not find any dated exterior photo of No. 949 from 2013–2019, so I could not honestly brief the old frontage "as it was". If the owner still wants the original, the honest caption is "The Humming Tree, 12th Main (2013–2019)"; both years are sourced. The available material is limited: the undated CollectiveProject roof-terrace photos (translucent steel-grid canopy, brick, planters) and the December 2021 Street View, which shows the building after closure with other tenants' signs on it.

2. The "big tree". No source says the old venue had a notable tree or that the name came from one. Only a rooftop terrace and rooftop stage are documented. The tree is the logo. The big street tree in the brief is the one in front of the new 100 Feet Road site in the March 2026 Street View; it is not a feature of the venue.

3. Signage. The sign on the new wall is in Kannada (ದಿ ಹಮ್ಮಿಂಗ್ ಟ್ರೀ). The tree emblem is the brand logo, so keep it simple or generic.

4. Reopening date. No source gives an exact day. The best range is between December 2025 (the Deccan Herald plan and the OpenStreetMap node added 25 Dec 2025) and 20 January 2026 (Homegrown: "is back").

5. Name confusion. Unrelated companies called "The Humming Tree" exist: Kamlesh Builders, a Chennai apartment project, and hummingtree.com, an architecture studio. Don't mix up their images.

6. Shared address. Subko runs a café at the same address ("Subko at The Humming Tree", reported 30 Sep 2026), so new photos may show Subko branding.

rameshwaram-cafe.name: The Rameshwaram Cafe (Indiranagar, 100 Feet Road)
rameshwaram-cafe.caption: The Rameshwaram Cafe, 100 Feet Road
rameshwaram-cafe.why: A popular Bengaluru South Indian tiffin chain known for ghee podi idli, benne dosa and filter coffee. It was founded in 2021 and began with a 700 sq ft outlet in Indiranagar (Indian Retailer, 10 Mar 2026: https://www.indianretailer.com/news/rameshwaram-cafe-opens-large-format-restaurant-churchgate). In November 2024 the Indiranagar branch reopened on 100 Feet Road in a 15,000 sq ft space for up to 400 guests, with a "temple-inspired design" (Bbtl News press text, 7 Nov 2024: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aQwmS2et9b0; The Federal, 18 Nov 2024, calls it a "brand-new, relocated branch": https://thefederal.com/category/features/rameshwaram-cafe-in-bengaluru-and-hosur-highway-156544). Locals know it for its queues: Swiggy, 25 Jun 2026, says "the queues are real" (https://blog.swiggy.com/order-food-online/best-masala-dosa-in-indiranagar/). Google review tags include "no seating" (227) and "standing room only" (147).

rameshwaram-cafe.brief:
Based on Google Maps photos: Sajid Ali Khan's forecourt panorama (dated Oct 2026), review photos by Chaithra Devadiga (about Sep 2026), Mrigna Narain (about Aug 2026) and virapara hiren (about Jul 2026), checked against Nov 2024 launch-video frames. The view is from the paved forecourt on 100 Feet Road, looking east.

A long single-storey pavilion stands on a raised grey granite plinth. In the middle, a wide flight of about eight stone steps with steel handrails climbs to its raised terrace. The terrace is edged with dark ornamental railings and large round grey pots of leafy shrubs. Two black stone bull (Nandi) sculptures, garlanded with marigolds, sit at the top of the steps on either side.

The long low canopy has a charcoal-grey awning with a scalloped fringe. Behind it a carved black fretwork frieze runs along the beam. Marigold swags hang along the front, and below them a row of brass temple bells on chains, each with a marigold tassel, among strings of fairy lights.

On the left, a tall black panel carries a lit eight-petal knot emblem and the Kannada name in three lines. On the right, a black wall carries the emblem and the English name. Behind the pavilion rises a taller block clad in dark grey square tiles, with the emblem above a bilingual name band near the top.

Foreground: grey pavers, a tree in a raised square black planter, a slim palm, wooden benches with black iron legs, a couple of short black posts and parked scooters. People stand on the terrace and steps, and a few sit on the benches and planter edges. Soft overcast daylight.

Leave out the police barricade, the No Smoking sign, the digital menu screens and the 2024 launch-day yellow drapes. Draw the signs name-only or with a simplified emblem.
rameshwaram-cafe.cautions:
1) Checks against the earlier note. Confirmed: deep paved forecourt, wide stone steps with steel handrails, raised terrace with dark railings and potted plants, black walls with the emblem and Kannada lettering, a tree in a raised square planter, scooters, people standing. Corrections: the canopy is not a plain flat pergola. It is a long low roof with a white/grey scalloped awning fringe, marigold swags and small lanterns; launch frames show a raised skylight ridge over the middle. The emblem is an eight-petal lotus outline around an interlaced knot, not a simple round mandala. The Kannada name (ದಿ ರಾಮೇಶ್ವರಂ ಕೆಫೆ) is on the left panel; a right-hand wall carries the English name. The note left out the taller dark grey tiled block behind, which carries a bilingual name band. "Bollards" are short black posts, and I could see only a few. "Eating standing" rests on the review tags and an Aug 2026 photo of standing counters, not on the exterior shots.
2) The 2024 blast happened at the Brookefield/Whitefield branch, not here. Keep it out of the caption and brief.
3) Do not draw from older photos. Many listings (magicpin, Justdial, the Google cover photo from Sep 2021) show the original 12th Main outlet, with its black corner-box fascia.
4) A Sep 2026 Google photo (user Kaliamoorthy) shows an ornate gold-on-black temple-style entrance (namam, conch, chakra, brass finials) below a white-tiled building. I could not match it to this exterior, so I left it out. It may be an inner entrance or another branch.
5) The Oct 2026 photo includes a yellow police barricade and a 'No Smoking – Bengaluru City Police' sign. I suggest leaving both out.
6) The emblem and name are brand marks; draw the signs name-only or simplify the emblem.
7) The opening year conflicts: Nov 2024 per press and news, 2025 per the official site.
8) Google photo URLs may expire. Review-photo dates are relative to 20 Oct 2026 and so approximate.

notDrawn.someshwara-temple: INTACH calls this Chola-period temple 'one of the oldest temples in Bengaluru', and Wikipedia describes its towering eastern gopuram as typical 16th-century work. It is one metro stop west of Indiranagar in Halasuru, and its gopuram is the most striking silhouette near the neighbourhood.
notDrawn.leela-palace: Open since 2001, this Mysore Palace-inspired hotel has domes, arches and nine acres of gardens. It is the grandest building on Indiranagar's southern edge (Kodihalli) and a citywide landmark.

reserves: Lavonne Cafe, Defence Colony: a respected pastry school and cafe since 2012, but the building is a modern box whose main feature is red neon script, which gets lost in one-colour ink. It would also be a second bakery next to Glen's.

Bhartiya Jalpan, 100 Feet Road at 13th Main: a long-running landmark, but it is only moderately iconic (3.6 on District, mixed reviews). Its drawing would rely on the shop lettering and a rain tree rather than the building.
